idiom_name: one map operation per context, bound by the two functor laws
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: for each context type define exactly one higher-order operation that takes the wrapped value(s) plus an ordinary A -> B function and returns the same kind of wrapper around B - an empty or failed context stays empty or failed and the function is not called. Give it the ecosystem's name for the operation (map, fmap, transform, Select) and keep the signature identical across contexts so helpers, decorators and validators can be written once against it. Treat the two laws as the instance's contract (map of the identity function changes nothing; map over a composition equals composing the maps) and test them once per instance instead of re-asserting behaviour at every call site. Keep the mapping function pure, because the functor decides whether and how often it runs - that is what makes the empty, lazy and asynchronous cases safe. Reach for bind/flatMap as soon as the mapping function itself returns a context.
code_sketch:
context F with one operation:
    map(F<A>, A -> B) -> F<B>          # empty/failed F passes through untouched

laws (the instance's contract; test them once):
    map(fa, identity)   == fa
    map(fa, f . g)      == map(map(fa, g), f)

rule of thumb:
    A -> B          -> map        (this pattern)
    A -> F<B>       -> bind       (monad: the next step depends on the value)
    F<A -> B>       -> apply      (applicative: independent contexts)
pitfalls: Writing map so that it also sequences or flattens: the operation then no longer satisfies the laws, and every generic function written against plain map breaks.
Sharing one mutable instance state across contexts instead of one instance per context type, so 'the functor' becomes a project-wide singleton with hidden behaviour.
Declaring the pattern implemented because a type has a method named map: without the identity and composition discipline the name promises more than the code provides.

In languages without typeclass instances (JavaScript, Python, Go), the name 'map' is a convention only: a method called map that reorders elements, drops the empty case, or runs the mapper twice compiles without error and silently violates the laws.

Passing an effectful mapper (I/O, mutation, logging) to map on a lazy or async context causes non-obvious timing: the effect runs once per element on the consumer thread, not at the call site, and skipped elements mean the effect never fires.

Using map instead of bind/flatMap when the mapping function returns a wrapped type (Option, Promise, Either) produces a nested context (F<F<B>>) that must be manually unwrapped — the smell is triple-nested types visible in compiler error messages.

In TypeScript without fp-ts HKT encoding, abstracting over a Functor requires Kind<F,A> wrappers or explicit interface definitions; a plain TypeScript generic cannot express 'F<_>' as a first-class kind, limiting reusable helper functions.

In JavaScript sparse arrays, map produces a sparse result even when the callback would produce a defined value for an absent slot — the result is Array hole, not undefined, and iterating it skips the slot entirely.

In Go, the nil pointer on a Result or Option is not the same as None/Err: calling .Map on a nil receiver panics in samber/mo, while a nil *Result may silently no-op in other implementations; always construct explicit None/Err values.
In Python with custom Option/Either wrappers, forgetting to implement map on a subclass breaks generic functions that expect it, producing a runtime AttributeError only when the empty branch is hit.
In C++, std::optional::transform is only available since C++23; on earlier standards the pattern must be emulated with if (opt) return opt.map(...) manually or with a boost::optional equivalent.

Confusing OCaml module functors with the categorical Functor (mappable types): OCaml functors are parameterised modules at the module level, not value-level mappings — they serve a different purpose and follow different laws.

Deriving Functor for a recursive type without handling the recursion correctly: a hand-rolled fmap for a tree that calls fmap recursively must apply f at the correct anchor point, not at every level indiscriminately — a common bug in hand-written Haskell or Scala instances.

Using map over a context that may be empty in a performance-critical hot path: each map allocates a new wrapper and the closure call overhead is measurable in inner loops — profile before optimising and only unroll if the profiler confirms it matters.

Implementing map on a type that has internal mutable state: lazy functors over mutable cells (IORef, STRef) can violate the composition law if the mapper observes or modifies shared state, making the laws not merely theoretical.

Treating map as a general-purpose for-each loop for side effects: using map for logging, mutation or I/O works in eager contexts but silently drops effects in lazy or async contexts, producing code that passes tests and fails in production.

Wrong move: treat Enum.map over an Elixir map as a structure-preserving functor -> it returns a list and breaks the map-shaped identity expectation -> instead map values with a map-preserving helper or use a lawful wrapper.
Wrong move: assume any method named map obeys the functor laws -> identity or composition can fail and generic rewrites become unsound -> instead state and property-test both laws for every instance.

Wrong move: use map to trigger a required effect on a lazy or deferred context -> the work may be skipped, deferred, or repeated by consumers -> instead sequence the effect explicitly at a terminal operation.
